stories.title: AV Management Nabs SoHo Mixed-Use for $43M
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the sale of 73-75 Sullivan St., a newly constructed mixed-use property totaling 32,957 square feet and comprising 11 residential units and a ground-floor commercial space anchored by The Montessori School. The final sale price was $43,333,000. A Cushman & Wakefield team of Dylan Walsh, Niko Nicolaou, Ryan Dowd and Andrew Berry represented the seller, 73-75 Sullivan Partners-1, LLC, and procured the buyer, AV Management. “This sale underscores the continued demand for high-quality multifamily assets in core Manhattan neighborhoods,” said Walsh. “The property’s fully free-market status and prime SoHo location generated strong investor interest, reflecting the enduring strength of New York’s multifamily investment market.” The property benefits from immediate access to multiple subway lines, including the C, E, 1 and 6 trains. Residents and commercial tenants enjoy proximity to world-class retail, dining and cultural destinations, as well as convenient access to parks, fitness centers and grocery stores, Cushman & Wakefield said. The post AV Management Nabs SoHo Mixed-Use for $43M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AV Management acquired 73-75 Sullivan St. SoHo mixed-use for $43.3M
11 residential units plus ground-floor Montessori School anchor; fully free-market
Prime Manhattan location near C, E, 1, 6 subway lines
stories.summary: AV Management purchased a newly constructed 32,957-sq-ft mixed-use property in SoHo for $43.3M, comprising 11 apartments and a ground-floor commercial space. The asset is fully free-market with immediate transit access. The transaction underscores continued institutional demand for core Manhattan multifamily despite competitive pricing.
stories.impact: SoHo pricing at ~$3.9M per residential unit signals sustained depth of capital for prime Manhattan infill; however, absence of density (11 units across 33k sq ft) reflects zoning constraints that limit development leverage in core neighborhoods. New development opportunity limited; resale/value-add the primary play.

stories.title: U.S. Multifamily Gains Momentum in Q2 2026 as Absorption Surges
stories.excerpt: The U.S. multifamily market gained momentum in the second quarter of 2026 as apartment demand accelerated and new construction continued to moderate, CBRE said Wednesday. Net absorption of 167,500 units nearly doubled the Q1 tally, while the national multifamily vacancy rate declined by 50 basis points quarter-over quarter to 4.3%, below its long-term average of approximately 5.0%. New supply growth continued to ease, with 77,700 units delivered in Q2 2026, a 14% decrease from a year earlier. Average monthly rent rose 0.5% year-over-year and 1.5% quarter-over-quarter to $2,257 in Q2 2026. Multifamily investment volume totaled $34.9 billion in Q2 2026, down 2.7% from a year earlier. Even so, the multifamily sector remained the largest property sector for commercial real estate investment during the quarter, accounting for 27% of total volume. “The supply wave in the U.S. multifamily sector is cresting, with deliveries down 14% year-over-year and absorption nearly doubling quarter-over-quarter,” said Kelli Carhart, Head of Multifamily Capital Markets for CBRE. “Multifamily is positioned for its strongest rent recovery since 2022.” The post U.S. Multifamily Gains Momentum in Q2 2026 as Absorption Surges appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Q2 2026: Net absorption 167,500 units, nearly doubled Q1; vacancy fell 50 bps to 4.3%
Deliveries moderated 14% YoY to 77,700 units; supply wave cresting nationally
Rents rose 0.5% YoY, 1.5% QoQ to $2,257; investment volume $34.9B (down 2.7% YoY)
stories.summary: U.S. multifamily absorption nearly doubled in Q2 2026 to 167,500 units while new deliveries declined 14% year-over-year to 77,700. Vacancy compressed 50 basis points to 4.3%, below the 5% long-term average. Rent growth accelerated to 1.5% quarter-over-quarter despite only 0.5% year-over-year gains, positioning the sector for strongest rent recovery since 2022.
stories.impact: With supply moderating sharply and absorption surging, the overbuilt multifamily cycle is definitively closing—creating a 12–24 month window for developers to acquire and underwrite stabilized assets before cap rates re-compress. Markets with pent-up demand and limited new supply in pipeline (e.g., Sunbelt secondary markets, coastal Tier-2s) are primed for accretive development starts in 2026–2027.

stories.title: Institutional Investor Snares San Dimas Light Industrial Park
stories.excerpt: SRS Real Estate Partners arranged the $41-million sale of San Dimas Commerce Center, a 19-building light industrial park located at 410-490 W. Arrow Hwy, in San Dimas. VP Dave Faris and EVP and senior managing principal Richard Schwartz represented the seller, San Dimas BP LLC. The buyer is an institutional investor with a national presence. Situated on 10.54 acres, San Dimas Commerce Center totals approximately 179,345 square feet and was 90% occupied at the time of sale. It is leased to more than 70 local and regional businesses, including several long-term occupants. “San Dimas Commerce Center offers the type of infill small-bay industrial product institutional investors seek but seldom have the opportunity to acquire,” said Faris. “The property combines diversified income from a broad tenant base with the long-term flexibility to sell individual buildings to owner-users. We built the marketing campaign around that optionality, and the strong response validated the strategy.” The post Institutional Investor Snares San Dimas Light Industrial Park appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Institutional investor acquired San Dimas Commerce Center for $41M
19-building light industrial park, 179,345 sq ft, 90% occupied on 10.54 acres
Diversified tenant base (70+ local/regional businesses); optionality for individual building sales
stories.summary: SRS Real Estate Partners brokered the $41M sale of San Dimas Commerce Center, a 19-building light industrial park totaling 179,345 sq ft with 90% occupancy across 70+ tenants. The institutional buyer values the infill location, long-term lease diversification, and flexibility to sell individual buildings to owner-users.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. Industrial infill with owner-user optionality appeals to a different capital class (yield-focused institutions) and markets than apartment development. However, signal of institutional capital chase for small-bay industrial suggests continued flight to supply-constrained, operational real estate—opposite of multifamily's supply-heavy environment.

stories.title: Morris Heights Seniors Housing Project Secures Permits
stories.excerpt: Permits have been approved for a new 10-story affordable senior housing development at 105 W. Tremont Ave. in the Morris Heights neighborhood of the Bronx. Developed by Crown Holdings in partnership with The Community Builders, one of the nation’s largest affordable housing organizations, the project will provide 95 Affordable Independent Residences forSeniors (AIRS) and form part of a broader neighborhood regeneration initiative in Morris Heights. Designed by Crown Architecture, the approximately 55,000-square-foot, 100-foot-tall building will bring housing and support services to a borough where demand for affordable homes outpaces supply. In addition to housing, residents will have access to onsite amenities and services that include community and recreational spaces, an outdoor patio and garden, consultation rooms, laundry facilities, bicycle storage and a 24-hour attended receptionThe project incorporates a strong sustainability agenda through its Passive House design standards. The all-electric building will also feature an approximately 1,800-square-foot rooftop solar array. The post Morris Heights Seniors Housing Project Secures Permits appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Crown Holdings & Community Builders permitted 95-unit affordable senior housing in Morris Heights Bronx
10-story, 55,000 sq ft, 100-ft tall; Passive House, all-electric design
Part of neighborhood regeneration; strong demand for affordable units outpaces supply in borough
stories.summary: Crown Holdings and The Community Builders secured permits for a 95-unit affordable senior housing development (AIRS) at 105 W. Tremont Ave. in Morris Heights, Bronx. The 55,000-sq-ft, 10-story building features Passive House design, all-electric systems, and community amenities. The project addresses acute affordable housing shortage in the borough.
stories.impact: Confirms Bronx affordability crisis and policy tailwind for senior/affordable multifamily; however, AIRS targeting seniors limits broader rental demand signal. Regulatory/entitlement tailwind (permits approved efficiently) suggests government appetite for affordable density. Minimal capital competition for affordable projects vs. market-rate; developer should monitor whether TIF, PILOT, or low-income housing tax credits (LIHTC) are enabling economics—if so, affordable pipeline may accelerate borough-wide.

stories.title: Fully Leased Chula Vista Retail Fetches $30M
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets arranged the $30.4-million sale of Terra Nova Plaza, a fully leased, 96,114-square-foot retail property positioned within a 301,000-square-foot regional shopping center in Chula Vista. Senior managing director Gleb Lvovich, managing director Daniel Tyner and senior managing director Geoff Tranchina. represented the seller, a global investment manager. Located at 390 E H St., Terra Nova Plaza sits within a high-performing grocery-anchored center. Dick’s Sporting Goods operates from a 44,477-square-foot space, while Floor & Decor occupies 51,637 square feet under long-term leases. Co-tenants within the larger center include Smart & Final, CVS, Marshalls, Chase Bank, Taco Bell, Jack In the Box and Shell. “The combination of long-term lease security, exceptional freeway visibility and proximity to one of the region’s most dynamic residential growth corridors made this an extremely compelling opportunity,” said Lvovich. “Chula Vista’s retail fundamentals remain strong with limited new supply and continued demand from quality tenants seeking high-traffic locations.” The post Fully Leased Chula Vista Retail Fetches $30M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JLL sold Terra Nova Plaza, fully leased retail for $30.4M in Chula Vista
96,114 sq ft within 301k-sq-ft center; Dick's Sporting (44k sf), Floor & Decor (51k sf) anchors
Long-term leases; grocery center; limited new retail supply; proximity to residential growth corridor
stories.summary: JLL Capital Markets sold Terra Nova Plaza, a fully leased 96,114-sq-ft retail asset anchored by Dick's Sporting Goods and Floor & Decor, for $30.4M. The property sits in a high-performing grocery-anchored center in Chula Vista with exceptional freeway visibility and proximity to a dynamic residential growth corridor.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance, but Chula Vista's retail fundamentals (strong demand, limited new supply) reflect underlying residential growth and density that favor new apartment development. Rising retail valuations and occupancy in fast-growth Southland submarkets signal demand tailwinds; apartment developers should prioritize Chula Vista/South County for mixed-use or infill multifamily sites capturing same demographic in-migration.

stories.title: TikTok Tells U.S. Employees to Return to Office 5 Days a Week
stories.excerpt: TikTok’s work-from-home era is scrolling to an end. The ByteDance-owned social media platform has instructed its U.S. employees to return to the office five days a week, sources told Business Insider. The change impacts the company’s hybrid employees that are currently allowed to work from home at least one day per week. TikTok alerted employees across several large divisions in December to expect a full office return in 2026, according to Insider, although certain teams, like TikTok’s e-commerce division, resumed five-day office attendance more than a year ago. TikTok employs thousands of U.S. employees across dozens of metro office locations, including its Culver City headquarters in Greater Los Angeles, and a seven-floor spread at the Durst Organization’s One Five One tower in Manhattan’s Times Square. TikTok earlier this month announced the closure of its 250-person Nashville office, however, just two years since opening. Return-to-office policies have been gaining ground across the country and across industries this year, Commercial Observer previously reported. U.S. office visits rose 6 percent year-over-year in the first half of 2026, and achieved the narrowest first-half gap from pre-pandemic levels thus far. The return-to-office wave has continued to buoy post-pandemic office leasing in cities like New York, where returning demand has driven rents to record highs this year. TikTok’s move to reign in work-from-home follows similar moves by its competitors Instagram and Amazon. Amazon’s office workers returned for five-day work weeks nearly two years ago, while other large technology companies, like YouTube and Patreon, have maintained their hybrid schedules. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: TikTok mandates 5-day office return in 2026 for hybrid US employees
Thousands of employees across metro offices: Culver City HQ, 7-floor spread in Times Square (151 tower)
Nashville 250-person office closed in December after ~2 years
stories.summary: TikTok has instructed U.S. hybrid employees to return to the office five days per week starting in 2026, affecting thousands across multiple metro locations. The company operates a major headquarters in Culver City, Los Angeles, and a seven-floor presence at the Durst Organization's One Five One in Times Square, Manhattan. TikTok recently shuttered its 250-person Nashville office.
stories.impact: RTO trend by major tech employers (TikTok, others in cycle) signals potential office stabilization and reduced remote work flexibility—but note TikTok's Nashville exit despite RTO, suggesting selective footprint optimization. For multifamily: NYC Times Square submarket may see marginal office-to-residential conversion opportunity if TikTok or similar tenants consolidate; however, Culver City expansion is more likely, supporting LA apartment demand near tech corridor.

stories.title: Blackstone Snaps Up Ken Griffin’s 125 Worth Avenue in Palm Beach for $86M
stories.excerpt: Billionaire Ken Griffin just parted ways with his last remaining retail property on Worth Avenue in Palm Beach, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned. Blackstone Real Estate has agreed to acquire the three-story office and retail building at 125 Worth Avenue, owned by Griffin since 2023, for $86 million in an all-cash deal, sources familiar with the trade said. Griffin previously bought the roughly 50,000-square-foot property from Dreyfuss Management and Frisbie Group for $83 million in 2023. “High-street retail continues to experience strong fundamentals, and Palm Beach represents one of the highest performing luxury retail markets in North America,” Elena Clarfield, principal at Blackstone Real Estate, told Commercial Observer. Indeed, as a retail corridor, the world famous Worth Avenue enjoys extreme scarcity when it comes to supply, coupled with soaring demand from a deluge of high-income residents into Palm Beach. Limited supply has also driven up property valuations in the prestigious area, evidenced by Acadia Realty Trust’s March 2026 acquisition of 225 Worth Avenue, leased to Gucci, for $43 million, or more than $4,329 per square foot. Blackstone declined to comment further but sources said the firm now intends to renovate the property, upgrading both the retail and office components to better align them with the continued evolution of Worth Avenue, a high-scale shopping district that’s home to several luxury tenants including Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Ferragamo and Van Cleef & Arpels. Representatives for Griffin could not immediately be reached for comment. The transaction represents Griffin’s second disposition on Worth Avenue in under a year. Last November, the billionaire sold his 48,578-square-foot property at 151 Worth Avenue to the family of GoldenTree Asset Management financier Steven Tananbaum, Commercial Observer reported at the time. bullets: Blackstone acquired 125 Worth Avenue Palm Beach for $86M in all-cash
Ken Griffin's 50k-sq-ft office/retail; purchased by Griffin in 2023 for $83M
Worth Avenue luxury retail scarcity; limited supply, high-income resident influx driving valuations
stories.summary: Blackstone Real Estate acquired 125 Worth Avenue, a 50,000-sq-ft office and retail building on exclusive Worth Avenue in Palm Beach, for $86M in an all-cash deal. Ken Griffin owned the property since 2023 (purchase price $83M). Worth Avenue enjoys extreme supply scarcity and strong fundamentals from affluent resident in-migration.
stories.impact: Limited multifamily impact. However, Palm Beach luxury retail strength and rapid property appreciation ($83M to $86M in 3 years) reflect broader wealth migration into South Florida—a core driver of Miami/Palm Beach apartment demand. Developers should track high-net-worth residential in-migration (signaled by retail capital intensity) as leading indicator of sustained multifamily rent growth and asset valuations in Palm Beach/Miami submarkets.

stories.title: Fund Administrator Hanover Park Inks 19K-SF Deal at 387 Park Avenue South
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven fund administrator is moving its headquarters to TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Avenue South, Commercial Observer has learned. Hanover Park signed a 19,269-square-foot lease on the entire 10th floor of the NoMad property, marking its fifth office move in two years, according to CEO Chris Hladczuk. The firm’s most recent office address is listed on its website as 115 East 23rd Street. TF Cornerstone did not immediately provide the asking rent or the length of the lease, but the average asking rent for office space in Midtown South was $85.73 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “Existing tenants are choosing to expand here and new companies are choosing to locate here,” Joe Lanzilotta, director of commercial asset management at TF Cornerstone, said in a statement. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” It is unclear who represented the tenant in the transaction, but Cushman & Wakefield’s Ethan Silverstein handled negotiations on behalf of the landlord in the deal signed in July. It’s unclear who represented the tenant. “The combination of TF Cornerstone’s long-term investment, highly efficient 20,000-square-foot floor plates and premier NoMad location continues to resonate with tenants,” Silverstein said in a statement. “The recent leasing activity demonstrates that companies are prioritizing best-in-class buildings, and with one full floor becoming available this fall, the property remains well positioned to meet continued demand.” Other recent deals in the 230,000-square-foot building at the corner of Park Avenue South and East 27th Street include a lease for marketing firm PMG Worldwide, which expanded from the second to third floor in May and brought its total footprint there to 38,744 square feet, according to TF Cornerstone. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI fund admin) signed 19.3k-sq-ft HQ lease at 387 Park Avenue South NoMad
10th floor entire; company's 5th office move in 2 years
Midtown South asking rent $85.73/sq ft (Q2 2026); existing tenants expanding, new firms locating
stories.summary: Hanover Park, an AI-driven fund administrator, leased 19,269 sq ft (entire 10th floor) at TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in NoMad as its fifth office move in two years. Market asking rents in Midtown South averaged $85.73/sq ft in Q2 2026. The landlord noted strong tenant retention and new business attraction.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily relevance. Office flight and frequent relocations signal ongoing tenant churn and space optimization (shrinking per-capita footprint), not stabilization. However, NoMad's appeal to high-growth tech/fintech firms supports residential demand from employees; developers should monitor if NoMad office supply tightens (it hasn't) to justify apartment density nearby—currently oversupplied office market.

stories.title: Peachtree Recaps Ritz-Carlton Portland With $141M C-PACE Loan
stories.excerpt: A New York lender is more than ready for a Portland hospitality resurgence. Ready Capital, which assumed full ownership of the The Ritz-Carlton Portland mixed-use project following a foreclosure in July 2025, just secured $141 million of commercial property accessed clean energy (C-PACE) debt for the recapitalization of the 35-story tower, Commercial Observer has learned. Peachtree Group originated the C-PACE loan for the 2023-completed Block 216 Tower development that features a 251-key hotel, 131 condominium units and 159,000 square feet of office space. Construction of the Ritz-Carlton-Portland, the Marriott’s brand’s first hotel in the Pacific Northwest, commenced in 2019 before encountering delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic and ensuing struggles to the city’s economy. Jared Schlosser, head of credit originations at Peachtree Group, said condo units at the property have sold at a healthy pace and the hotel is well positioned for success as one of the newest lodging offerings in the Portland region. “It’s the nicest hotel up there and that pocket of Portland is revitalizing,” Schlosser told CO. “I think there’s probably more tailwinds ahead versus headwinds for Portland.” Schlosser added that C-PACE debt was conducive for the recap since as a newer building it was developed under “stringent” building codes with much of the project eligible for retroactive financing. He noted that the deal marks Peachtree’s second largest loan. Ready Capital set the stage for owning The Ritz-Carlton Portland when it acquired a prior construction loan on the development valued at more than $500 million through a 2022 merger with Mosaic Real Estate Investors. The lender manages the property in partnership with Lincoln Property Company. Ready Capital did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Ready Capital (foreclosure owner) closed $141M C-PACE loan for Ritz-Carlton Portland recap
Block 216 Tower: 251-key hotel, 131 condos, 159k sq ft office; completed 2023
Condo units selling at healthy pace; hotel positioned for success as newest regional lodging
stories.summary: Ready Capital, which acquired the Ritz-Carlton Portland through foreclosure in July 2025, secured $141M in commercial property-assessed clean energy (C-PACE) financing for the 35-story Block 216 Tower. The mixed-use development includes a 251-key hotel, 131 condos, and 159,000 sq ft of office space completed in 2023. Condo sales are tracking well and the hotel is positioned for recovery as the region's newest luxury property.
stories.impact: Portland hotel/mixed-use distress followed by recapitalization signals regional market recovery post-COVID; however, limited multifamily signal (condos != rental apartments). Note: C-PACE financing availability (144% of asset value) suggests lenders' willingness to refinance quality mixed-use assets, supporting capital availability for non-distressed development. Portland residential developers should monitor condo absorption and tourism recovery as proxy for rental demand stabilization.

stories.title: Office Furniture Manufacturer Haworth Renews 30K SF at SL Green’s 125 Park Avenue
stories.excerpt: Office furniture manufacturer Haworth is staying seated at 125 Park Avenue. Haworth has signed a 10-year lease renewal for its 30,365-square-foot office and showroom space at the 25-story Midtown office building, landlord SL Green Realty announced Wednesday. The company, which manufactures and sells high-end, ergonomic office seating and workspaces, has been a tenant in the property, also known as the Pershing Square Building, for more than a decade. The firm, which did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment, previously renewed its lease for the same space back in 2015, CO reported at the time. The asking rent was $100 per square foot. SL Green was represented in-house in this deal, while Haworth was represented by Ethan Silverstein and Amy Zhen from Cushman & Wakefield. C&W did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “We are proud to extend our valued relationship with Haworth at 125 Park Avenue,” Steven Durels, executive vice president and director of leasing and real property at SL Green, said in a statement. “The building’s proximity to Grand Central Terminal and our new lobby and elevator cab renovation have helped maintain 99 percent occupancy.” SL Green acquired 125 Park Avenue in 2010 for $330 million, according to property records. The building sits across the street from Grand Central Terminal on Park Avenue and East 42nd Street. Other tenants in the building include banking and investment firm TD Securities and real estate brokerage Newmark. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Haworth (office furniture mfr) renewed 30,365-sq-ft lease at 125 Park Avenue for 10 years
SL Green Midtown office; tenant for 10+ years; previously renewed 2015
Proximity to Grand Central; new lobby/elevator improvements noted by landlord
stories.summary: Haworth, a high-end office seating and workspace manufacturer, signed a 10-year lease renewal for 30,365 sq ft of office and showroom space at SL Green's 125 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. The company has occupied the space for over a decade and previously renewed in 2015. SL Green highlighted the building's Grand Central proximity and recent lobby/elevator upgrades.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily relevance. Long-term renewal of office/showroom space by established tenant signals Midtown office stability for specific user types (furniture, fintech, services) but does not offset broader office oversupply. No conversion/adaptive reuse signal. Apartment developers should note Midtown office remains tenant-selective; density and transit access support mixed-use, but single-asset office tenancy does not signal broad sectoral pivot.
